newsitem.title: USA: Congress, Clinton head for disaster aid showdown.
newsitem.headline: Congress, Clinton head for disaster aid showdown.

text.p: Congress stood ready Thursday for a showdown with President Clinton over a bill providing emergency disaster relief for 35 states that he has vowed to veto as soon as it reaches his desk.

Republican leaders of both the House and Senate refused to remove two provisions Clinton has said he will not accept -- the first to avert another government shutdown and the second to block the use of sampling in the 2000 census.

Both the House and Senate scheduled votes on the $8.6 billion spending bill and passage was expected. Once Clinton has vetoed it, it was expected to make a quick U-turn back to Capitol Hill where it will be stripped of Republican-backed provisions and sent back to him for his signature.

"My hope is that the Republicans will keep the car running. Because it isn't going to take long to turn this car around, bring the bill back here, strip out the language," Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, Democrat of South Dakota, said.

Republicans, still smarting from the public blame they took for two government shutdowns in 1995, sought to prevent that from happening again this fall. They proposed to continue spending past the Oct. 1 start of the new fiscal year whether or not money bills have been passed.
But Democrats and the administration objected that this would give Republicans no incentive to negotiate with them on regular spending bills.

On the census issue, Republicans were eager to keep the traditional house-by-house count used for decades. Their opponents said the party feared its electoral strength could weaken in key districts if sampling, a statistical procedure designed to adjust for undercounting minorities, is used.
The Census Bureau, backed by a National Science Foundation study, said the sampling would provide a more accurate count of minorities.

After the House-Senate conference cleared the bill with the objectionable provisions intact, Clinton issued another veto threat Wednesday. "If the Republican majority is set on this course of adding contentious and extraneous provisions, they should send this bill as quickly as possible," he said in a statement. "I will veto it as soon as it arrives."
The president said he will return the bill to Congress swiftly "so they can send me a clean disaster assistance bill immediately that keeps aid flowing to those in need."
"Americans in need should not have to endure this unnecessary delay," he said.
The bill provides $5 billion in disaster aid for more than 30 states, $1.9 billion to pay for military operations in Bosnia and Iraq and money for other government agencies.
